Sentence meaning: “That restaurant is famous for its ramen.”

default.q.n4-type-1-q5-5.why.2: (c) とごう is incorrect because 都 is misread as と. Although it is read と in words such as 都市（とし） and 都会（とかい）, 都合 is read つごう.
default.q.n4-type-1-q5-5.why.3: (d) つこう is incorrect; 都 is correctly read as つ, but the voicing of 合 to ご is omitted.

Meaning of the sentence: "I will take the Japanese exam next month."

Sentence meaning: “Please wait a moment.”

default.q.n4-type-1-q11-11.why.1: (b) 持って is incorrect because 持つ is read as もつ (to hold or carry), not まつ.

Meaning: "My older sister works at a bank."

default.q.n4-type-1-q13-13.why.3: (d) 好 is incorrect because it means “to like, good,” not a noun referring to a person.
default.q.n4-type-1-q14-14.explanation:
Meaning: "The post office is on the right side of this road."
石・若・右・古 all have the 口 radical at the bottom and simple strokes above it, so beginners may confuse them when writing. However, only 右 is read みぎ.

default.q.n4-type-1-q14-14.why.2: (c) 右 is correct: read みぎ, meaning "right-hand side."
default.q.n4-type-1-q14-14.why.3: (d) 古 is incorrect because 古い means “old,” is read as ふるい, and not みぎ.
default.q.n4-type-1-q15-15.explanation:
Meaning: "Go straight along this road."
通・近・道・遠 all contain the 辶 radical, associated with going and movement, so they look similar. However, only 道 means "road" and is read みち.

default.q.n4-type-1-q15-15.why.1: (b) 近 is incorrect because 近い means “near” and is read ちかい, not みち.
default.q.n4-type-1-q15-15.why.2: (c) 道 is correct: read みち, meaning "road."
default.q.n4-type-1-q15-15.why.3: (d) 遠 is incorrect because 遠い means “far,” is read as とおい, and not みち.

default.q.n4-type-1-q16-16.explanation:
Meaning: "It was raining heavily, so the bus just wouldn't come."
Pattern: なかなか + verb in the negative form (来なかった) = "does not happen easily, just won't happen."
default.q.n4-type-1-q16-16.why.0: (a) なかなか is correct: 「なかなか＋negative」 means “not easily” or “for a long time without,” appropriately describing a bus that takes a long time to arrive because of heavy rain.

default.q.n4-type-1-q17-17.why.2: (c) しめて is incorrect because 閉める is a transitive verb meaning “to close,” so both the meaning and usage are wrong.
default.q.n4-type-1-q17-17.why.3: (d) しまって is incorrect because 閉まる is an intransitive verb meaning "to close," which is the opposite of the sentence's meaning.

Sentence meaning: "This book is easy, so even first-time readers can read it."

default.q.n4-type-1-q23-23.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 親切な.

default.q.n4-type-1-q24-24.verdict: The correct answer is (a). とても.

Meaning: "I caught a cold last week, so I had a doctor prescribe medicine for me at the hospital."

default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.verdict: The correct answer is (a). 少しずつ.
default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.explanation:
Sentence meaning: “My Japanese gradually improved.”
だんだん and 少しずつ both describe a change that takes place gradually over time.
default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.why.0: (a) 少しずつ is correct: it means "little by little, gradually," matching だんだん in the sentence.
default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.why.1: (b) すぐに means 'immediately,' which is opposite to 'gradually' (だんだん, implying a gradual process rather than an instant change).
default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.why.2: (c) たくさん means “a lot” and indicates quantity; it cannot express a gradual process of change.
default.q.n4-type-1-q26-26.why.3: (d) やっと means “finally,” describing an outcome achieved after waiting for a long time, unlike だんだん, which means “gradually.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.verdict: The correct answer is (c). とつぜん.
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.explanation:
Sentence meaning: “The sky suddenly grew dark, and then it began to rain heavily.”
急に and とつぜん both describe something that happens suddenly and without warning.
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.why.0: (a) だんだん means "gradually," expressing the opposite rate of change from 急に, which means suddenly.
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.why.1: (b) ときどき means “sometimes,” indicating repeated frequency rather than suddenness.
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.why.2: (c) とつぜん is correct: it means "suddenly," matching 急に (unexpectedly, without warning).
default.q.n4-type-1-q27-27.why.3: (d) やっと means “finally,” expressing a result after waiting; it differs from “suddenly” or “unexpectedly.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is (b). だいじな.
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.explanation:
Meaning: "This is a precious watch that my family gave me."
大切な and だいじな both describe something important and cherished.
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.why.0: (a) べんりな means "convenient" and is unrelated to the meaning "important, precious."
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.why.1: (b) だいじな is correct: it means "important" or "precious" and is closest in meaning to 大切な.
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.why.2: (c) ゆうめいな means “famous,” which is completely different from “important, valuable.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q28-28.why.3: (d) じゆうな means “free,” which is unrelated to the meaning of the sentence.
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.verdict: The correct answer is (d). きっと.
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.explanation:
Meaning: "Since you promised, you absolutely have to come tomorrow, okay?"
かならず and きっと both emphasize CERTAINTY, with no exceptions.
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.why.0: (a) たぶん means “perhaps” or “probably” and expresses a guess; it is less certain than かならず, which means “certainly” or “must.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.why.1: (b) ときどき means "sometimes" and indicates frequency; it is unrelated to the idea of "certainty."
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.why.2: (c) すこし means “a little,” indicating degree or quantity, so it is unrelated.
default.q.n4-type-1-q29-29.why.3: (d) きっと is correct: it means “surely” or “certainly,” and is closest in meaning to かならず, emphasizing certainty or a firm commitment.
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.verdict: The correct answer is (c). できるだけ.
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.explanation:
Meaning: "For my health, I try to walk as much as possible."
なるべく and できるだけ both express trying to do something to the GREATEST EXTENT possible.
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.why.0: (a) たまに means "occasionally"; it does not mean "to try one's best."
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.why.1: (b) もちろん means “of course” and is unrelated to “making every effort.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.why.2: (c) できるだけ is correct: it means "as much as possible" or "to the greatest extent possible," matching なるべく.
default.q.n4-type-1-q30-30.why.3: (d) ぜんぜん means “not at all” or “completely (not)” and is usually used with a negative form, so it does not fit the meaning here.
default.q.n4-type-1-q31-31.explanation:
「やっと」expresses that something awaited or difficult was finally achieved or happened. It is commonly used with a specific event that has been completed, and is not used for repeated actions or future predictions.
Example: 三年間勉強して、やっとN4に合格した。(After studying for three years, I finally passed N4.)
default.q.n4-type-1-q31-31.why.0: (a) "朝ごはんを食べて、やっと学校へ行きました" is incorrect because やっと carries the nuance of finally achieving something after difficulty or waiting. "I ate breakfast and went to school" is simply a normal sequence of actions, with no difficulty or waiting involved.
default.q.n4-type-1-q31-31.why.1: (b) "明日はやっと休みです" is incorrect because やっと is not used for a simple future event that has not yet happened; it is used for something that has already been achieved.
default.q.n4-type-1-q31-31.why.2: (c) "三時間も待って、やっとバスが来ました" is correct: やっと expresses finally achieving something that was expected or difficult after waiting for the bus for three hours.
default.q.n4-type-1-q31-31.why.3: (d) "田中さんは毎日やっと勉強しています" is incorrect because やっと is not used for a repeated daily action or habit. It is used for a single event achieved after difficulty or waiting.
default.q.n4-type-1-q32-32.explanation:
「届く」is an intransitive verb (something arrives on its own), whereas 「届ける」is a transitive verb (someone brings or delivers something). When the sentence has an object marked by ...を and a recipient marked by に, 届ける must be used, not 届く.
Examples: 手紙が届きました。(The letter arrived.)／手紙を届けました。(I delivered the letter.)
default.q.n4-type-1-q32-32.why.0: (a) 「母は毎朝、私に新聞を届きます」 is incorrect because 母 is the person performing the action of delivering the newspaper to “me.” The transitive verb 届けます must be used, not the intransitive verb 届きます.
default.q.n4-type-1-q32-32.why.1: (b) "先週注文した本が、今日届きました" is correct: 届く is an intransitive verb, so it is appropriate when the subject itself arrives at its destination—in this case, the book.
default.q.n4-type-1-q32-32.why.2: (c) "弟にたんじょうびのプレゼントを届きたいです" is incorrect because the implied subject, “I,” wants to DELIVER a gift to a younger brother (the object 「プレゼントを」and recipient 「弟に」). The transitive verb 届けたい must be used, not 届きたい.
default.q.n4-type-1-q32-32.why.3: (d) "荷物を明日までに届きますので" is incorrect because the subject delivers the luggage, and 「荷物を」 is the object. The transitive verb 届けます must be used, not the intransitive verb 届きます.
default.q.n4-type-1-q33-33.explanation:
「そろそろ」expresses that it is nearly time to do something. It refers to the present and commonly occurs with a volitional verb in the present form, for an action that has not yet happened. It is not normally used with a definite past time.
Example: もう9時だ。そろそろ寝よう。(It is already 9 o’clock. It is about time we went to bed.)
default.q.n4-type-1-q33-33.why.0: (a) "3年前、そろそろ日本に来ました" is incorrect because そろそろ does not go with a definite PAST time reference such as "3年前". そろそろ indicates that something is about to happen from the present, not an event that already happened in the past.
default.q.n4-type-1-q33-33.why.1: (b) "あの店のラーメンはそろそろおいしいです" is incorrect because そろそろ is used before an action or change that is about to occur, not before a static state expressed by an adjective such as "delicious."
default.q.n4-type-1-q33-33.why.2: (c) "きのう、そろそろ雨が降りました" is incorrect, as in (a), because そろそろ is not used with a definite past time such as “yesterday” and a completed past event.
default.q.n4-type-1-q33-33.why.3: (d) Correct: "遅くなったから、そろそろ帰りましょう" is appropriate. そろそろ signals that it is about time to do something (go home) from the moment of speaking, and the tense and context are correct.
default.q.n4-type-1-q34-34.explanation:
「なかなか」has two main uses: (1) with an affirmative adjective or verb, it emphasizes a considerable or unexpectedly high degree, meaning “quite” or “surprisingly”; (2) with a negative form, it means “not easily,” “hardly,” or “cannot seem to.” It is not normally used by itself before an ordinary affirmative action verb.
Example: この漢字はなかなか覚えられない。(I just cannot seem to memorize this kanji.)
default.q.n4-type-1-q34-34.why.0: (a) "弟はなかなか宿題をやりました" is incorrect because this is simply an affirmative statement about a completed action; it has neither the negative nuance nor the degree of emphasis needed for なかなか to modify it.
default.q.n4-type-1-q34-34.why.1: (b) "この店のラーメンはなかなかおいしいです" is correct: なかなか＋a positive adjective means “quite” or “surprisingly,” emphasizing a degree higher than expected.
default.q.n4-type-1-q34-34.why.2: (c) "明日はなかなか晴れるでしょう" is incorrect because it is an ordinary confident prediction, without a negative nuance or emphasis on degree.
default.q.n4-type-1-q34-34.why.3: (d) "今朝はなかなか朝ごはんを食べました" is incorrect because, as with (a), a simple affirmative action does not fit the usage of なかなか.
default.q.n4-type-1-q35-35.explanation:
「気がつく」means "to realize or notice" something (commonly used with ...ことに気がつく／...に気がつく). It cannot replace action verbs such as "do," "graduate," or "open."
Example: 財布を家に忘れたことに、駅で気がついた。(I realized at the station that I had left my wallet at home.)
default.q.n4-type-1-q35-35.why.0: (a) "母は毎日、晩ご飯を気がつきます" is incorrect because the intended meaning is “make/cook dinner,” but 気がつく means “notice” or “realize,” not “make something.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q35-35.why.1: (b) "来年、大学を気がつきます" is incorrect because the intended meaning is “graduate,” but 気がつく was mistakenly used; the two meanings are completely unrelated.
default.q.n4-type-1-q35-35.why.2: (c) Correct: "傘を持ってこなかったことに、家を出てから気がつきました". 気がつく means “to realize” or “to notice” a fact—in this case, that one had forgotten to bring an umbrella—and is used correctly.
default.q.n4-type-1-q35-35.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「先生は毎朝、教室のドアを気がつきます」 is wrong because the intended meaning is “open” the door, but 気がつく means “notice/realize” and does not describe physically acting on an object.
default.q.n4-type-1-q36-1.explanation:
Meaning: "I eat while watching TV."
Grammar point: 「Vます-stem + ながら」 expresses two simultaneous actions, and the subject must be the same person.
default.q.n4-type-1-q36-1.why.0: (a) 見 is correct: 「〜ながら」 always attaches to the ます-stem, formed by removing ます (見ます → 見), and expresses two actions taking place at the same time.
default.q.n4-type-1-q36-1.why.1: (b) 見て is incorrect because 「〜ながら」 does not attach to the te-form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q36-1.why.2: (c) 見る is incorrect because 「〜ながら」 does not attach to the dictionary form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q36-1.why.3: (d) 見た is incorrect because 「〜ながら」 does not attach to the past form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 話してはいけません.
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.explanation:
Meaning: "You must not speak loudly in the library."
～てはいけません expresses a PROHIBITION, which fits the rules commonly found in libraries.
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.why.0: (a) 話してもいいです (“it is permitted to speak loudly”) contradicts the library rule (speaking loudly is not allowed).
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.why.1: (b) 話してはいけません is correct: “You must not speak loudly,” which matches the library rule.
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.why.2: (c) 話さなくてもいいです (“you do not have to speak loudly”) implies that speaking loudly is optional; it does not correctly express the prohibition intended by the sentence.
default.q.n4-type-1-q37-2.why.3: (d) 話さなければなりません ('must speak loudly') is completely contrary to the context, since the library requires silence.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 泳げます.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.explanation:
Sentence meaning: "Can you swim in this river?"
Grammar point: Distinguishing the four forms of 泳ぐ — plain, potential, causative, and passive. A question about whether someone can swim must use the potential form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.why.0: (a) 泳ぎますか is the polite form asking about the action “Do you swim?” It asks about the action itself, not whether one can or may swim in this river.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.why.1: (b) 泳げますか is correct: it is the potential form, asking whether someone “can swim,” in terms of ability or safety, which fits the context of asking about a specific river.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.why.2: (c) 泳がせますか is the causative form, asking “Will you make someone swim?” It does not fit the context.
default.q.n4-type-1-q38-3.why.3: (d) 泳がれますか (passive form) is unnatural here and does not fit a question about the ability to swim.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.verdict: The correct answer is (d). 聞きながら.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.explanation:
Meaning: "I studied while listening to music."
～ながら attaches to the masu-stem (聞き＋ながら) to express two actions performed simultaneously by the same subject.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.why.0: (a) 聞き is only the verb stem from the masu-form and lacks the particle needed to indicate a simultaneous action, so the sentence is grammatically incomplete.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.why.1: (b) 聞いて (the て-form) expresses sequential actions (listen first, then study), not two actions occurring simultaneously as ながら does.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.why.2: (c) 聞くと with と expresses an automatic condition or result; it does not express simultaneous actions.
default.q.n4-type-1-q39-4.why.3: (d) 聞きながら is correct: ながら expresses two actions occurring simultaneously, as in “studying while listening to music.”
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.verdict: The correct answer is (c). 着た.
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.explanation:
Meaning: "I have worn a kimono once before."
The pattern ～たことがある (have done something before) always requires a verb in the plain past form immediately before it.
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.why.0: (a) 着る (dictionary form) is incorrect because ～ことがある, when expressing experience, requires the verb in the plain past form (た形), not the dictionary form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.why.1: (b) 着て (te-form) is incorrect because an experience pattern requires the plain past た-form, not the te-form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.why.2: (c) 着た is correct: the ordinary past form is used before ことがある to express the experience of having worn a kimono.
default.q.n4-type-1-q40-5.why.3: (d) 着ます (the polite form) cannot directly combine with ことがある in this pattern; the plain past form 着た must be used.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.verdict: The correct answer is (a). 前に.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.explanation:
Meaning: "In Japan, people say いただきます before eating."
Grammar point: 「Nの前に」 = before doing something. The following clause describes a fixed action associated with the start of a meal, so only 前に is appropriate.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.why.0: (a) 前に is correct: 「いただきます」 is said immediately BEFORE starting a meal, so 「食事の前に」 is used.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.why.1: (b) 後で is incorrect because after finishing a meal, Japanese people say 「ごちそうさまでした」, not 「いただきます」.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.why.2: (c) 間に is incorrect because 「間に」 indicates an ongoing period (while eating), not a starting point.
default.q.n4-type-1-q41-6.why.3: (d) うちに is incorrect because 「うちに」means “while a state still lasts,” as in 熱いうちに食べる, and does not fit here.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 上手な.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.explanation:
Sentence meaning: "Since Tanaka is Japanese, he is probably good at Japanese."
Rule before はず: plain-form verbs/i-adjectives + はず; nouns/na-adjectives + な + はず.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.why.0: (a) 上手 is used as-is, so it lacks the required な particle between the na-adjective and はず.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.why.1: (b) 上手な is correct: a na-adjective must add な before the noun-like form はず, according to the grammar rule.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.why.2: (c) 上手だ (だ-form) does not combine directly with はず in this way; だ must be removed and な added.
default.q.n4-type-1-q42-7.why.3: (d) 上手の is incorrect with the particle の because の connects nouns to nouns; it is not used after this type of na-adjective.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 降る.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.explanation:
Meaning: "According to the news on TV, apparently it will snow tomorrow."
そうです in its hearsay usage, meaning "I hear that..." or "apparently," attaches to the plain form of a verb without changing the verb's form.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.why.0: (a) 降り, the masu-stem used by itself, cannot precede そうです in this hearsay construction.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.why.1: (b) 降る is correct: the dictionary form plus そうです expresses hearsay (“I hear that...”), which fits because the information comes from a TV news report, and 明日 (“tomorrow”) requires a present or future reference.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.why.2: (c) The te-form 降って cannot be combined with そうです in the hearsay pattern.
default.q.n4-type-1-q43-8.why.3: (d) 降った is the past form, which conflicts with 明日 ('tomorrow'—an event that has not happened), so it does not fit the time logic.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 帰らせて.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.explanation:
Meaning: “I’m sorry, but my child is sick today, so please let me leave early.”
～させてください is a pattern used to ask permission to do something, often in the workplace. The preceding reason shows that the speaker is the person asking for permission.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.why.0: (a) 帰って is incorrect in this context: 「帰ってください」 asks someone else to leave, whereas the speaker is asking permission to leave because their child is ill.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.why.1: (b) 帰らせて is correct: causative + て + ください means “please allow me to go home,” which is the appropriate pattern for asking a superior for permission.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.why.2: (c) 帰られて is passive or honorific language; it does not express asking for permission.
default.q.n4-type-1-q44-9.why.3: (d) 帰らせられて is the passive causative form (being forced to go home), completely contrary to the speaker’s intention.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.verdict: The correct answer is (b). のに.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.explanation:
Meaning: "Although I studied a lot, my test score was still terrible."
のに expresses a result contrary to the normal expectation, unlike ので/から, which express a straightforward cause-and-effect relationship.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.why.0: (a) ので (“because”) expresses a straightforward cause-and-effect relationship, such as “because I studied a lot, I got good grades.” However, this sentence has the opposite result—poor grades despite studying a lot—so it is incorrect.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.why.1: (b) のに is correct because it expresses a contrast with expectations: although the person studied a lot, the score was still poor. This matches the logic of the sentence.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.why.2: (c) から (“because”), like ので, expresses a straightforward cause and does not fit a result that contradicts it.
default.q.n4-type-1-q45-10.why.3: (d) し (“and; furthermore”) is used to list additional reasons; it does not express contrast or surprise.
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.verdict: The correct answer is (b). ように.
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.explanation:
Sentence meaning: "I wrote it down so that I would not forget."
Rule: Use ために for a purpose with a volitional verb; use ように for a purpose involving a non-volitional verb, ability, or negative form (such as わすれない).
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.why.0: (a) ために is incorrect because it is used with affirmative volitional verbs for intentional actions, whereas 「わすれない」(not forget) is a negative, non-volitional verb that is not directly under one’s control, so ように must be used.
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.why.1: (b) ように is correct: it is used to express purpose with potential-form, non-volitional, or negative verbs (such as わすれない、できる、わかる...), so it is grammatically appropriate here.
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.why.2: (c) そうに ("seems like") describes an apparent appearance and does not express purpose.
default.q.n4-type-1-q46-11.why.3: (d) みたいに (“like”) expresses similarity, not purpose.
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.verdict: The correct answer is (b). 食べてみて.
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.explanation:
Meaning: "I followed the new recipe. Try it and see if it tastes good."
Grammar point: 「〜てみる」— to try doing something. A clue is a clause stating something that needs to be checked, such as 〜かどうか.
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.why.0: (a) 食べて is simply an invitation to eat; it cannot express the meaning of trying something to verify the proposition in the preceding clause (おいしいかどうか).
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.why.1: (b) 食べてみて is correct: 「〜てみる」 means “to try doing something and see what happens,” matching 「おいしいかどうか」 (“whether it is delicious”).
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.why.2: (c) 食べてある is incorrect because 「〜てある」describes a resulting state after an action and cannot be used with ください.
default.q.n4-type-1-q47-12.why.3: (d) 食べておいて is incorrect because 「〜ておく」 means doing something in advance to prepare for a later event, not trying something for evaluation.
default.q.n4-type-1-q48-13.explanation:
Meaning: "This bag is so heavy that I cannot carry it."
Rule for combining ～すぎる (too much) with an i-adjective: Remove い and add すぎる to the stem.
default.q.n4-type-1-q48-13.why.0: (a) 重く, the く-form, is used before ordinary verbs such as 重くなる; it is not used directly before すぎる.
default.q.n4-type-1-q48-13.why.1: (b) 重い is incorrect because the い-ending must be removed before adding すぎる; the full adjective cannot be retained.
default.q.n4-type-1-q48-13.why.2: (c) 重くて (て-form) is used to connect clauses and cannot be placed directly before すぎる.
default.q.n4-type-1-q48-13.why.3: (d) 重 is correct: when combining すぎる with an i-adjective, remove い and keep only the stem — 重い→重すぎる. This is grammatically correct.
default.q.n4-type-1-q49-14.verdict: The correct answer is (d). コップを.
default.q.n4-type-1-q49-14.explanation:
